purpose: Exploratory concept sketches; existing site unchanged

concepts.title: 01 / The visual handbook
concepts.prompt:
Use case: ui-mockup. Create a landscape 1536x1024 product concept sketch board for an easy-to-understand New Zealand first-home buyer educational website. This is a genuine UX exploration, NOT a finished landing page. Big meaningful illustrations, few words, instantly obvious controls. Premium pencil-and-ink design sketch on warm ivory paper, restrained rust-orange marker accents, dark charcoal type, editorial serif headings and highly readable simple sans labels. Detailed but economical hand-drawn architectural and everyday-object illustrations, intentional whitespace. Flat front-on screen wireframes with handdrawn borders; no perspective computer/device renders. A large main screen should occupy roughly two thirds of the board; one smaller follow-up screen on the right demonstrates the next interaction. A tiny handwritten arrow connects the states. Only 2 short marginal annotations. Design must be usable and concept-specific, not generic SaaS, dashboard cards, chatbots, giant paragraph blocks, fake stats, purple gradients, unexplained icon buttons or decorative blobs. No personal readiness score, lending approval, financial promises or invented interest rates. Preserve generous readable text, sparse labels. Render exact requested text cleanly. This is for adults new to buying a home, not for children. Include board title upper left and small label 'CONCEPT SKETCH · FIRST HOME NZ'.
Concept: an illustrated reference book, organised around real questions. NO fictional protagonist, NO map or game-world hotspots, NO timeline. Main screen is an elegant visual contents page titled "What do you want to understand?" Six large spacious illustration-and-question pairs in a 3 by 2 editorial grid, with subtle horizontal rules but NO boxed cards. Illustrations carry most of the space. Pair one engraved balance scale with suitcase versus home with "Rent or buy?"; savings jars and a KiwiSaver-labelled document with "Where does the deposit come from?"; house atop iceberg with "What does it really cost?"; a building inspector with torch with "What should I check?"; lawyer's fountain pen and contract with "What am I signing?"; keys and toolbox with "What happens after?". Top small header "A place of your own" and visible search field labelled "Find a question". Right follow-up screen, titled "The price is only the start", is dominated by a big iceberg with small house above water and three clean labels below water: "Rates", "Insurance", "Repairs". Beneath visual one short sentence "Budget for life after the keys." A small bottom disclosure row "Costs explained +", another "Checklist +", another "Official sources ↗". Back control clearly labelled "← All questions". A thin arrow from the cost iceberg tile to the follow-up screen. Margin notes exactly "Browse, don't follow a course" and "One picture explains one idea". The layout should feel like a beautifully illustrated field encyclopedia. Do not invent dense small text.

Concept: a visual decision workbench. One understandable question, two large visual alternatives, consequences shown graphically. Entirely different from a book grid or numbered chapters. Main screen title "Rent or buy?" Two equal generous columns: left "Keep renting" with a beautiful ink drawing of a suitcase, rented apartment and moving van; right "Buy a home" with ink drawing of a modest NZ weatherboard home, keys and maintenance toolbox. Between columns thin handdrawn vertical dividing line. Three aligned trade-off rows with small meaningful pictures and exceptionally short labels: renting "Easier to move", "Landlord handles major repairs", "Rent keeps going"; owning "More control", "Repairs are yours", "Loan + ownership costs". At bottom two large clear outlined buttons "Explore renting" and "Explore buying". One top-left breadcrumb "Your options"; top-right compact "All questions". Right follow-up screen shows selecting buying, titled "Could the monthly cost fit?" One big illustrated monthly money tray, clear separate piles labelled "Loan", "Rates", "Insurance", "Repairs", with unspent-space label "Room for life". NO amounts or proportions that imply real data. A short sentence "The bank's maximum isn't your target." Button "See the full budget →" and a small "Details & sources +" disclosure. The visual hierarchy is illustration first, comparison second, one action third. Margin notes exactly "See the trade-off" and "No right-answer quiz". Avoid checklist-board or spreadsheet aesthetics. Limit text to prescribed labels.

Concept: a simple illustrated route map, making the whole NZ home buying process visible at once. NOT a 3D village, NOT hotspots covering a house, NOT ten equal chapter tabs. Main screen titled "How do I get the keys?" A single clean winding ink route with five clearly numbered large stations running from left-to-right in two tidy rows; each stop anchored by a meaningful generous illustration. Stations: "1 Work out your money" (savings jar and calculator); "2 Build your team" (lender, lawyer and inspector bust sketches); "3 Find & check a home" (magnifying glass over a weatherboard house); "4 Agree the deal" (pen signing paper); "5 Get the keys" (key and open door). Use charcoal route lines, rust selected station 3; every station readable, no dense menus. Below the main line, one lighter dotted connector between money, checks and deal with tiny label "Some checks happen together". Side note near station 4 with simple warning flag, exact text "Auction? Do the checks before bidding." Top right small "Find a question". Right follow-up screen titled "Before you commit", one large cutaway house drawing, underneath three plainly labelled evidence objects: report "Building", council folder "Records", shield "Insurance". Bottom button "Open the viewing checklist →", small disclosure "Why these checks matter +", source link "Official guidance ↗", and a clearly visible "← Whole journey". Arrow from selected station to detail screen. Margin notes exactly "Know where you are" and "Keep the whole process in view". The art should communicate route and dependencies, not adventure-game decoration. Large drawings and extremely concise copy.

Concept: practical pocket companion organised by the situation the buyer is in, not by a fictional story or textbook chapters. Main desktop screen title "What are you doing today?" Four huge illustrated entry choices in an airy two-by-two arrangement, minimal borders: a person and lender across a desk "Talking to the bank"; a person opening a house door "At a viewing"; hands holding sale papers and pen "Making an offer"; keys with moving box "Getting the keys". Small unobtrusive header link "Just starting? See the basics" and visible search "Ask a question". Emphasise the "At a viewing" choice with a small rust underline. Right follow-up screen styled as a simple mobile-height content panel, not a rendered device. Title "At a viewing" with short subheading "Look up. Then look closer." Huge clear sketch of a ceiling with a water stain and roof/gutter context, a small rust circle draws attention to the stain. Two plain action lines "Look for water marks." and "Ask about leaks and repairs." Bottom has three tidy labelled controls "What to look for", "What to ask", "What to request". A clear next-cue control "Next: damp & ventilation →", a "Save to my checklist" control, and a quiet "Why it matters & sources +" disclosure. Small visible "1 of 6" indicates finite viewing prompts, not a readiness/completion score. Margin notes exactly "Useful in the real situation" and "One thing to notice at a time". Make the right-screen ceiling illustration prominent; do not overcrowd it with labels. This should feel like an illustrated practical companion rather than a task-management dashboard.
